name: Uruguayan Spanish
notes: Uruguayan Spanish. Rioplatense base: žeísmo/šeísmo for ⟨ll⟩/⟨y⟩ (devoicing trend toward [ʃ] in younger speakers). Less extreme than Buenos Aires in some features. Border dialects show Portuguese influence (DPU — Dialectos Portugueses del Uruguay). ⟨LL⟩ AND ⟨Y⟩: both are [ʃ] before a vowel (calle [ˈkaʃe], yo [ˈʃo]). Lipski (2018, p. 502): «In most of Argentina and Uruguay, /j/ has traditionally been realized as a voiced fricative, [ʒ], but devoicing to [ʃ] has extended from Buenos Aires and Montevideo to much of the remaining territory.» The devoiced [ʃ] is the value that sentence gives for the present-day spread; [ʒ] is the older value. SESEO: ⟨c⟩ before ⟨e i⟩ is [s], the same phoneme as ⟨z⟩. Lipski (2011, p. 4): «The opposition /s/-/θ/ is not found in the Canary Islands (where seseo is the norm), nor in any part of Latin America.»

Reproduces the Lipski (1994) geographical dialect-zone classification of Latin American Spanish (list (2)): Mexican/SW-US; Caribbean; Guatemala-Yucatan-Costa Rica; El Salvador-Honduras-Nicaragua; interior Colombia + highland Venezuela; Pacific coast Colombia/Ecuador/Peru; Andean (Ecuador/Peru/Bolivia/NW-Argentina/NE-Chile); Chile; Paraguay/NE-Argentina/E-Bolivia; Argentina/Uruguay. Used here to enumerate the regional zones; no phonology quoted.
